title: Concept of environmental assessment
summary: This subchapter is largely Nepali law, and the single most important update is that the Environment Protection Act 2076 (2019) replaced the 1997 Act and introduced a THIRD tier — the Brief Environmental Study — below IEE and EIA. Learn the process sequence and the approving authority for each tier, because both are examined directly. The mitigation hierarchy (avoid, minimise, rectify, compensate) is the other reliable item, and its point is that avoidance ranks first because it is achieved at the design stage and costs least.

sections.heading: The legal framework in Nepal
sections.body:
**The current law is the Environment Protection Act, 2076 (2019)**, with the **Environment Protection Rules, 2077 (2020)**. It **replaced** the Environment Protection Act 2053 (1997) and its Rules 2054 (1997), and the change matters because questions set from older material give the superseded position.

**The most significant change: THREE tiers, not two.**

| Tier | Full name | For | Approved by |
|---|---|---|---|
| **BES** | **Brief Environmental Study** | The **smallest** category of proposals | The **concerned body** (local or provincial level, per the schedule) |
| **IEE** | **Initial Environmental Examination** | Intermediate proposals | The **concerned ministry** |
| **EIA** | **Environmental Impact Assessment** | The **largest and most sensitive** proposals | The **Ministry of Forests and Environment** |

The **BES** is the 2019 Act's addition — a lighter study for small proposals that previously either needed a full IEE or fell outside the system entirely. It reflects the practical recognition that a proportionate response is better than an all-or-nothing threshold.

**Which tier applies** is determined by **schedules to the Rules**, which list proposals by **sector and by threshold** — capacity, area, cost, length, or population served. A road of a given length, a hydropower project above a given capacity, a water supply scheme above a given population all fall into a defined tier. Additionally, **any proposal in an environmentally sensitive area** (a national park, conservation area, wetland, historic or cultural site, or a densely populated area) is **elevated to a higher tier** regardless of its size.

That elevation rule is worth remembering: the tier depends on **both the scale of the proposal and the sensitivity of the location**, not on scale alone.

**Institutional roles:**

| Body | Role |
|---|---|
| **Ministry of Forests and Environment (MoFE)** | Approves **EIA**; the apex environmental authority |
| **Concerned ministry** | Approves **IEE** for its sector |
| **Provincial and local government** | Approve **BES**; roles expanded under federalism |
| **Department of Environment** | Monitoring and enforcement |
| **Proponent** | Prepares the report, implements the EMP, and remains responsible |

**Other relevant instruments:**

| Instrument | Governs |
|---|---|
| **Environment Protection Act 2076 / Rules 2077** | The EIA/IEE/BES system, pollution control, environmental standards |
| National EIA Guidelines 1993 | Procedural guidance (still referenced) |
| **Forest Act 2076** | Forest clearance; a project on forest land needs separate approval |
| **Land Acquisition Act 2034** | Compulsory acquisition and compensation |
| **Solid Waste Management Act 2068** | Waste responsibilities |
| **Local Government Operation Act 2074** | Local authority environmental functions |
| Water Resources Act, Electricity Act | Sectoral licensing, in which environmental clearance is a condition |

**Why the environmental clearance matters commercially, not just legally.** It is a **condition precedent** to the license, the loan and the construction permit. A project that begins work without it is liable to be **stopped**, and its expenditure becomes irregular. For an engineer, the practical consequence is that the environmental study belongs at the **feasibility stage**, in parallel with the technical investigation — not as a document produced afterwards to satisfy a formality. A study done late either delays the project or, worse, rationalises decisions already taken.

sections.heading: The EIA process
sections.body:
**The sequence** — and questions ask for it in order:

> **Screening → Scoping → Terms of Reference → Baseline study → Impact prediction and evaluation → Mitigation → Environmental Management Plan → Report → Public review → Approval → Implementation → Monitoring → Auditing**

**Screening and scoping are distinct, and the distinction is examined:**

| Stage | Question answered |
|---|---|
| **Screening** | **WHETHER** an assessment is needed, and at **which tier** (BES, IEE or EIA) |
| **Scoping** | **WHAT** the assessment must cover — which issues, which area, which alternatives, which methods |

So screening is a **gateway decision** made against the schedules; scoping **defines the work**. Scoping is the more consequential of the two for study quality, because an issue omitted at scoping will not be assessed — and it is the stage at which the **Terms of Reference** are drawn up and approved.

**Public consultation is mandatory**, and at two points:

1. At **scoping**, when a **public notice** is published and written comments are invited from the affected community, the local government, schools and health posts;
2. On the **draft report**, which must be made **publicly available** with a further opportunity to comment, and a **public hearing** held in the affected area.

**Recommendations from the concerned local government** must accompany the report — a federalism-era requirement giving local bodies a formal voice.

**Why consultation is substantive rather than procedural.** The affected community holds information no consultant can obtain from documents: which spring the village actually uses, which trail floods, which grazing land matters, which site is culturally significant. A study that skips genuine consultation produces mitigation measures that do not address the real impacts — and generates the local opposition that stops projects later, at far greater cost.

**Baseline study** establishes the **existing condition** against which impacts are judged, across four environments:

| Environment | Components |
|---|---|
| **Physical** | Air quality, noise, water quality and quantity, soil, geology, land use, climate |
| **Biological** | Flora, fauna, aquatic life, forests, **protected and endangered species**, habitats |
| **Socio-economic** | Population, occupation, income, health, land ownership, infrastructure, employment |
| **Cultural** | Religious and historic sites, archaeology, traditional practices, aesthetics |

The baseline must cover a **full annual cycle** where seasonal variation matters — river flow and water quality above all, since a study based on monsoon data alone misses the dry-season condition that usually governs.

**Impact prediction and evaluation.** Each impact is characterised by:

| Attribute | Categories |
|---|---|
| **Nature** | Beneficial or **adverse** |
| **Magnitude** | High, medium, low |
| **Extent** | Site-specific, local, regional, national |
| **Duration** | Short, medium, **long term** |
| **Reversibility** | Reversible or **irreversible** |
| Timing | Construction phase or operation phase |
| Type | **Direct, indirect, cumulative** |

**Cumulative impacts** are the ones most often missed and increasingly emphasised: a single small hydropower scheme may have modest effects, but **a cascade of schemes along one river** dewaters most of its length. Assessing each in isolation therefore misses the actual impact, which is why basin-level or **Strategic Environmental Assessment (SEA)** is applied to plans and programmes rather than individual projects.

**Methods of impact identification**, examined by name:

| Method | Character |
|---|---|
| **Checklist** | Simple, comprehensive; no interactions shown |
| **Matrix (Leopold)** | Actions against components; shows **magnitude and importance** |
| **Network** | Traces **indirect and secondary** effects through chains of cause |
| **Overlay / GIS** | Spatial; excellent for **alignment and siting** decisions |
| Ad hoc, expert judgement | Rapid, but not transparent |

The **network method** is the one that reveals **indirect** effects: a road does not merely occupy land, it enables access, which enables settlement and logging, which causes deforestation — a chain no checklist captures.

**Analysis of alternatives** is a required part of an EIA and is the most valuable part in practice, because the greatest environmental gains come from choosing a different **site, alignment, technology, scale or timing** — not from mitigating a fixed design. The **no-project alternative** must also be considered as the baseline against which the others are judged.

sections.heading: Mitigation, management and monitoring
sections.body:
**The mitigation hierarchy** — in strict order of preference:

| Rank | Measure | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **1. AVOID** | Prevent the impact entirely | **Change the site or alignment**; shift a road away from a forest or a settlement |
| **2. MINIMISE** | Reduce the magnitude | Dust suppression, noise barriers, silt traps, timing work outside the breeding season |
| **3. RECTIFY / RESTORE** | Repair the affected environment | Reinstate borrow pits, replant cleared areas, restore drainage |
| **4. COMPENSATE / OFFSET** | Provide equivalent value elsewhere | Compensatory afforestation, resettlement, cash compensation |

**Avoidance ranks first for two reasons**, and the reasoning is the examinable part: it is the **only measure that is certain** — a impact avoided cannot fail to be mitigated — and it is achieved at the **design stage, where it costs least**. Once construction begins, avoidance is no longer available and only the weaker options remain.

**Compensation ranks last because it does not prevent the harm.** Planting trees elsewhere does not restore the habitat destroyed here; paying a household does not restore its land. Compensation is legitimate for residual impacts that cannot be avoided or reduced, and illegitimate as a substitute for avoidance that was available and not taken.

**The Environmental Management Plan (EMP)** converts the assessment into an implementable document, and it must state for every mitigation measure:

> **WHAT** is to be done · **WHERE** and **WHEN** · **WHO** is responsible · **HOW MUCH** it costs · **HOW** its effectiveness will be verified

An EMP without an allocated **budget** and a named **responsible party** is not a plan — and that is the commonest defect in practice. The mitigation cost must appear in the **project cost estimate**, not as an aspiration.

**Monitoring** — three kinds, and each answers a different question:

| Type | Question |
|---|---|
| **Baseline monitoring** | What was the **condition before**? |
| **Compliance monitoring** | Are the **committed measures being implemented**, and are standards being met? |
| **Impact (effects) monitoring** | Are the **predicted impacts actually occurring**, and are the measures **working**? |

**Impact monitoring is the one that closes the loop**, because it tests whether the prediction was right. Without it, an EIA is an untested forecast and the discipline never learns.

**Environmental auditing** is conducted after the project is operating — under the Nepali Rules, typically **two years after operations begin** — to evaluate the **actual** impacts against those predicted, the effectiveness of mitigation, and compliance with the approved EMP. Its findings should feed back into the design of similar projects, which is the mechanism by which assessment practice improves.

**Common failures of EIA in practice**, worth knowing because they are the profession's own critique:

| Failure | Consequence |
|---|---|
| Prepared **after** the design is fixed | Alternatives cannot be considered; the study rationalises decisions already taken |
| Treated as a **permit-obtaining formality** | Mitigation is listed and not implemented |
| **Poor baseline data**, one season only | Impacts cannot be predicted or later verified |
| **Cumulative impacts ignored** | Basin-scale effects missed entirely |
| **No monitoring or auditing** | Predictions never tested; no learning |
| **Consultation nominal** | Local knowledge lost; opposition emerges later |
| **No budget** for the EMP | Measures are unfunded and unexecuted |

The honest professional position is that an EIA is worth what its **implementation and monitoring** are worth, and that the engineer's responsibility does not end when the approval is obtained.

sections.heading: Pollution, standards and specific environmental issues
sections.body:
**Air pollution.** The principal pollutants and their chief sources:

| Pollutant | Main sources | Effects |
|---|---|---|
| **PM₁₀ and PM₂.₅** | Combustion, **road dust**, **brick kilns**, construction | **Respiratory and cardiovascular disease**; PM₂.₅ reaches the alveoli |
| **SO₂** | Coal, brick kilns, diesel | Respiratory irritation, acid rain |
| **NOₓ** | **Vehicles**, combustion | Respiratory effects, ozone and smog formation |
| **CO** | **Incomplete combustion** | Binds haemoglobin; deadly indoors |
| Hydrocarbons, VOCs | Vehicles, solvents | Ozone precursors |
| Ground-level ozone | Secondary, from NOₓ and VOCs | Respiratory effects |
| Lead | Historic (leaded petrol) | Neurotoxic |

**Kathmandu Valley's air pollution** has a specific and instructive mechanism. The valley is a **bowl surrounded by hills**, and in winter a **temperature inversion** forms: a layer of warm air sits above cooler air near the ground, so the atmosphere is **stable** and vertical mixing stops. Pollutants from **vehicles, brick kilns, road dust and waste burning** are then **trapped** in a shallow layer, and concentrations build up over days until a weather change disperses them.

That is why the problem is **seasonal and worst in winter mornings**, why it cannot be solved by taller stacks (which do not penetrate the inversion), and why the only effective responses are **reducing emissions at source** — cleaner vehicles and fuel, improved or relocated brick kilns, paved and swept roads, and a ban on waste burning.

**Standards** are set by the **National Ambient Air Quality Standards for Nepal, 2069 (2012)**, with vehicle emission standards (Nepal Vehicle Mass Emission Standards) and industry-specific limits.

**Water pollution** — sources and their character:

| Source | Character |
|---|---|
| **Point source** | A **identifiable discharge** — sewer outfall, industrial pipe. **Easier to regulate and treat** |
| **Non-point (diffuse) source** | **Spread over an area** — agricultural runoff (fertiliser, pesticide), urban runoff, erosion. **Far harder to control** |

The distinction matters for policy: point sources yield to **permits and treatment plants**; non-point sources require **land management practices**, which are much harder to enforce. As point sources are progressively controlled, non-point sources come to dominate the remaining pollution — which is the situation in most developed catchments now.

**Noise pollution.** Measured in **dB(A)**, on a logarithmic scale — so a **10 dB increase is perceived as a doubling of loudness**, and adding two equal sources gives only **+3 dB**. Nepali standards set limits by zone:

| Zone | Day | Night |
|---|---|---|
| Industrial | 75 | 70 |
| Commercial | 65 | 55 |
| **Residential** | **55** | **45** |
| Silence zone (hospital, school) | 50 | 40 |

Control at the **source** (quieter plant, mufflers), along the **path** (barriers, distance, enclosure — noise falls 6 dB per doubling of distance from a point source), or at the **receiver** (glazing, ear protection). Source control is always preferable, and construction noise is managed chiefly by **restricting working hours**.

**Solid waste management.** The hierarchy, in order:

> **Reduce → Reuse → Recycle → Recover (energy/compost) → Dispose**

**Sanitary landfilling is the only acceptable disposal method**, and its essential components are worth listing because a question may ask what distinguishes it from a dump:

| Component | Function |
|---|---|
| **Liner** (clay or geomembrane) | Prevents **leachate** reaching groundwater |
| **Leachate collection and treatment** | Removes and treats the contaminated liquid |
| **Gas venting or collection** | Manages **methane**, which is explosive and a strong greenhouse gas |
| **Daily cover** of soil | Controls odour, flies, rodents, litter and fire |
| **Monitoring wells** | Confirm groundwater is not contaminated |
| **Final capping and after-use** | Restores the site |

**Open dumping, open burning and river discharge are all unacceptable**, whatever the local practice: dumping contaminates groundwater with uncontrolled leachate and breeds disease vectors; burning releases **dioxins and particulates**; river discharge destroys the water source. Nepal's **Solid Waste Management Act 2068 (2011)** makes management a local government responsibility.

**Nepal-specific environmental issues** that appear in questions:

| Issue | Character |
|---|---|
| **Landslides and soil erosion** | Steep young geology, deforestation, road construction; **the dominant environmental hazard** |
| **Deforestation and forest degradation** | Fuelwood, encroachment, road access |
| **Kathmandu Valley air quality** | Inversion, vehicles, brick kilns |
| **River pollution (Bagmati, Bishnumati)** | Untreated sewage and solid waste; minimal dry-season dilution |
| **Glacial retreat and GLOF risk** | Climate change; a design flood case unique to the high mountains |
| **Biodiversity and protected areas** | Projects in national parks and conservation areas face the strictest scrutiny |
| **Resettlement and land acquisition** | Hydropower and road projects; socially the most contentious issue |
| Indoor air pollution | Biomass cooking; a major rural health burden |

**Road construction deserves the closing note** because it is where a Nepali civil engineer most directly causes or prevents environmental harm. A hill road built without care produces far more damage than its own footprint: **spoil tipped down the slope** buries fields and blocks streams, **uncontrolled drainage** triggers landslides, and **cut slopes left unprotected** erode for years. The mitigation is well established and inexpensive — **controlled spoil disposal in designed tips**, **cross drainage and catch water drains built before the monsoon**, **bio-engineering of cut and fill slopes**, and **construction sequenced to avoid working through the monsoon**. That these measures are known and often omitted is exactly why environmental assessment exists, and why the engineer's professional obligation extends beyond the pavement to the slope it sits on.

formulas.label: The three tiers in Nepal (EPA 2076/2019)
formulas.expression: BES → concerned body ;   IEE → concerned ministry ;   EIA → Ministry of Forests and Environment
formulas.note: BES is the 2019 Act's addition. Tier depends on BOTH scale and location sensitivity.

formulas.label: EIA process sequence
formulas.expression: Screening → Scoping → ToR → Baseline → Prediction → Mitigation → EMP → Report → Public review → Approval → Monitoring → Auditing
formulas.note: SCREENING decides whether and at what tier; SCOPING decides what the study must cover.

formulas.label: Mitigation hierarchy
formulas.note: Avoidance ranks first because it is certain and is achieved at the design stage, where it costs least.

formulas.label: EMP requirements
formulas.expression: For each measure: what, where, when, WHO is responsible, HOW MUCH it costs, how it is verified
formulas.note: An EMP without a budget and a named responsible party is not a plan. The cost belongs in the project estimate.

formulas.label: Types of monitoring
formulas.expression: Baseline (what was) ; Compliance (are measures implemented) ; Impact (are predictions correct)
formulas.note: Impact monitoring closes the loop by testing the prediction. Auditing typically 2 years after operations begin.

formulas.label: Noise addition (logarithmic)
formulas.expression: Two equal sources give +3 dB ; a 10 dB rise is perceived as a doubling of loudness ; −6 dB per doubling of distance
formulas.note: Residential limit in Nepal: 55 dB(A) day, 45 night.

formulas.label: Solid waste hierarchy
formulas.note: Sanitary landfill requires a liner, leachate collection, gas venting, daily cover and monitoring wells.

formulas.label: Point and non-point sources
formulas.expression: Point: identifiable discharge, controllable by permit and treatment. Non-point: diffuse, needs land management.
formulas.note: As point sources are controlled, non-point sources come to dominate the remaining pollution.
